title: Build a Sentence
lines: Build a Sentence opens the Writing section. You see a short exchange: one person says something, and the reply is given as a set of word chunks in the wrong order. You put the chunks in the correct order to make one natural, grammatical sentence. It is a fast test of English word order.
## What is on the screen
- A line from the first speaker, for example a question from a classmate or a comment from a coworker.
- Below it, the reply with empty slots and a group of 4-7 chunks (single words or short phrases). Some words of the reply may already be in place.
- You drag or tap the chunks into the slots. You can move them again before you go on.
- Sometimes one chunk does not belong. You must leave this extra chunk out.
## Timing and scoring

There are 10 items, and the whole set takes only a few minutes (about 6 minutes in this app's mock). That is roughly 30-35 seconds per item. Each item is right or wrong: the whole sentence must be in the correct order to score. The Writing section as a whole takes about 23 minutes, together with the email and the academic discussion.
## What is being tested
- Question word order: auxiliary before subject ("Have you finished ...?", "Where did she put ...?").
- Embedded (indirect) questions: no inversion after "Do you know", "Can you tell me", "I wonder" ("Do you know where the lab is?", not "where is the lab").
- Tenses and auxiliaries: present perfect, past continuous, future with will and going to, modals.
- Adverbs of frequency and time: before the main verb but after "be" ("She usually takes the bus", "He is always late").
- Relative clauses: "the book that I borrowed", "the student who sits next to me".
- Passive voice: "The results will be posted on Friday."
- Prepositional phrases and set patterns: "interested in", "depends on", "not only ... but also".
## Method, step by step
- Step 1: Read the first speaker's line and decide what the reply does: answers a question, accepts, refuses, asks back, gives information.
- Step 2: Look at the chunks and find the anchor: the subject and the main verb. Every sentence is built around them.

- Step 3: Check whether the reply is a statement or a question. A question mark at the end, or a question word in the chunks, tells you it is a question; then the auxiliary probably comes before the subject.
- Step 4: Place the fixed partners together: auxiliary and main verb, preposition and its object, adjective and noun, "not only" with "but also".
- Step 5: Put time and place phrases at the end, usually place before time ("at the library on Monday").
- Step 6: Check for an extra chunk. If one chunk duplicates a function (two auxiliaries, two prepositions) or has the wrong form, leave it out.
- Step 7: Read the whole sentence in your head. It should sound like something a person would say.
## Worked example 1: an embedded question
> Speaker: The printer on this floor is broken again.
> Chunks: is / do you / the nearest / one / know / where
> Reply: Do you know where the nearest one is?

After "Do you know", the question becomes a statement: question word, subject, verb. So "where the nearest one is", not "where is the nearest one". The question mark comes from "Do you know", which keeps normal question order.
## Worked example 2: adverb position and an extra chunk
> Speaker: How do you get to campus?
> Chunks: the early bus / I / take / usually / am / because of my 8 a.m. class
> Reply: I usually take the early bus because of my 8 a.m. class.
"usually" goes before the main verb "take". The chunk "am" is the extra: "I am usually take" is wrong because "take" needs no auxiliary in the simple present. The reason phrase goes at the end.
## Worked example 3: relative clause and passive
> Speaker: Did you hear anything about the scholarship?
> Chunks: the students / who / applied / will be / in May / contacted
> Reply: The students who applied will be contacted in May.

The subject is "the students who applied" (a relative clause right after the noun it describes). The verb is passive, "will be contacted", because the students receive the action. The time phrase goes last.

! If two orders seem possible, choose the more neutral, common one. Time phrases at the very start are possible in English, but in these items the time phrase usually goes at the end unless a chunk with a capital letter shows otherwise.
## Common traps
- Inverting inside an embedded question ("Can you tell me when does the store open?").
- Putting an adverb of frequency after the main verb ("I take usually").
- Separating a phrasal verb or set phrase wrongly ("look the word up" is fine, "look up it" is not; "depends on", not "depends of").
- Using the extra chunk because it seems to add meaning. Every correct sentence uses the right chunks only.
- Forgetting agreement: a singular subject with "has", a plural one with "have".
- Not reading the first speaker's line: the reply must answer it in a natural way.
## How to practise between mocks
- Revise the grammar points above one at a time, then write five sentences of your own for each.
- Take sentences from your reading, write each one on paper, cut it into chunks and rebuild it the next day.
- Practise turning direct questions into indirect ones: "Where is the gym?" becomes "Could you tell me where the gym is?"
- Learn adverb positions with simple models: "I always", "I have never", "She is often".
- Do sets of 10 items against the clock, aiming for about 30 seconds each, then review the grammar point behind every mistake.
